paragraphs.heading: Going there, not just looking
paragraphs.text: Space exploration means physically investigating outer space, either with robot probes that carry no crew or through human spaceflight. People were studying objects in the sky long before reliable written history. Actually going there only became possible once large, fairly efficient rockets were built in the mid-twentieth century. The usual reasons given include science, national prestige, bringing countries together, the long-term survival of humanity, and military advantage.

paragraphs.heading: The Space Race
paragraphs.text: The early years were driven by a Space Race, with the Soviet Union and the United States competing to prove their technology was better. The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first human-made object to orbit Earth, on 4 October 1957. It also flew the first human into space, Yuri Gagarin on Vostok 1 in 1961, and saw the first spacewalk, by Alexei Leonov in 1965. The United States answered by landing Apollo 11 on the Moon on 20 July 1969.

paragraphs.heading: Before orbit
paragraphs.text: Rockets reached space years before the first successful orbital launch in 1957. On 20 June 1944 a German V-2 test launch called MW 18014 climbed to 176 kilometers, well above the Kármán line. It did not have orbital speed, so it fell back and crashed, becoming the first sub-orbital spaceflight.

paragraphs.heading: Sputnik and Gagarin up close
paragraphs.text: Sputnik 1 weighed about 83 kg and carried two radio transmitters whose beeps could be heard on radios around the world. Studying those signals gave information about the electron density of the ionosphere. The satellite burned up when it came back down on 3 January 1958. Gagarin's flight on 12 April 1961 went once around the globe in about 1 hour and 48 minutes.

paragraphs.heading: Reaching the Moon and planets
paragraphs.text: Luna 2 reached the Moon in 1959, the first artificial object to arrive at another celestial body, and Luna 9 made the first soft landing there in 1966. Six crewed spacecraft landed on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. Probes then flew past the other planets: Mars in 1965, Jupiter in 1973, Mercury in 1974, Saturn in 1979, and Uranus and Neptune with Voyager 2 in 1986 and 1989. In 2015 Dawn went into orbit around the dwarf planet Ceres and New Horizons passed Pluto.

paragraphs.heading: Venus leads the way
paragraphs.text: The first flyby of another planet was Venera 1 past Venus in 1961, though Mariner 2 in 1962 was the first Venus flyby to send back data. Venus was also the first planet to send data from its surface: Venera 7 landed in 1970 and transmitted for 23 minutes. In 1975 Venera 9 returned the first pictures taken on the surface of another planet, again Venus.

paragraphs.heading: From rivalry to partnership
paragraphs.text: In the 1970s attention moved from one-off flights toward renewable hardware such as the Space Shuttle, and from rivalry toward cooperation. The best example is the International Space Station, built between 1998 and 2011. The 2000s saw national programs in China, the European Union, Japan and India move forward, and the 2010s saw private companies build launch vehicles, capsules and satellites in earnest. In the 2020s the two leading programs both aim at the Moon: the U.S.-led Artemis program and the International Lunar Research Station, led by China.
